questions.stem: Which component of blood is responsible for producing antibodies?
questions.explanation: Lymphocytes are white blood cells that recognise a specific antigen and manufacture antibodies against it, giving the body immunity. Phagocytes, the other main group of white cells, destroy bacteria by engulfing them instead.

distractorRationale.a: Red cells carry oxygen and have no nucleus, so they cannot make protein
distractorRationale.c: Platelets initiate clotting at a wound
distractorRationale.d: Fibrinogen is a clotting protein; the antibody-producing cell is the lymphocyte

questions.stem: The absence of a nucleus in a mature red blood cell is an advantage because it

options.text: allows the cell to divide more rapidly
creates more space for haemoglobin, so more oxygen can be carried
makes the cell able to produce antibodies

questions.explanation: The nucleus occupies a large part of a typical cell, so losing it frees volume that can be filled with haemoglobin. It also makes the cell more flexible, so it can bend through narrow capillaries.

distractorRationale.a: Without a nucleus the cell cannot divide at all
distractorRationale.c: The cell still respires, though only anaerobically since it has no mitochondria
distractorRationale.d: Antibodies are made by lymphocytes, which do have nuclei

questions.stem: In the lungs, haemoglobin combines with oxygen to form
questions.explanation: Where oxygen concentration is high, as in the alveolar capillaries, haemoglobin binds oxygen loosely to form bright red oxyhaemoglobin. In respiring tissue, where oxygen is low, the compound dissociates and releases oxygen to the cells.

distractorRationale.a: Carboxyhaemoglobin is formed with carbon monoxide and is almost irreversible
distractorRationale.c: Methaemoglobin is an altered form of haemoglobin that cannot carry oxygen
distractorRationale.d: Hydrogencarbonate ions are how most carbon dioxide is carried, in the plasma

questions.stem: A patient of blood group A needs a transfusion. Which of the following units of blood can safely be given?

options.text: Any group, since all human blood is compatible

questions.explanation: Group A plasma contains anti-B antibodies, so any donor cell carrying antigen B would be agglutinated. Group O red cells carry neither A nor B antigen, so there is nothing for the recipient's antibodies to attack, which is why group O is the universal donor.

distractorRationale.a: Group B cells carry antigen B, which the recipient's anti-B would agglutinate
distractorRationale.b: Group AB cells carry both antigens, including B, so they too would be agglutinated
distractorRationale.d: Mismatched transfusion causes agglutination and can be fatal

questions.stem: Group AB is described as the universal recipient because AB blood

options.text: has no antigens on its red cells
has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies in its plasma
contains more haemoglobin than other groups
clots more slowly than other groups

questions.explanation: Compatibility depends on whether the recipient has an antibody against the donor's antigens. AB plasma has neither anti-A nor anti-B, so red cells of any ABO group can be received without agglutination.

distractorRationale.a: AB cells carry both A and B antigens; it is group O that has none, making it the universal donor
distractorRationale.c: Haemoglobin content does not vary with blood group
distractorRationale.d: Clotting rate is unrelated to ABO group

questions.stem: During blood clotting, the soluble plasma protein fibrinogen is converted into insoluble fibrin by
questions.explanation: Platelets release thrombokinase, which with calcium ions and vitamin K converts prothrombin to thrombin. Thrombin then acts on fibrinogen, turning it into a mesh of fibrin threads that traps blood cells and forms the clot.

distractorRationale.b: Haemoglobin transports oxygen and takes no part in clotting
distractorRationale.c: Insulin is a hormone that lowers blood glucose
distractorRationale.d: Pepsin is a protein-digesting enzyme in the stomach

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to run a petrol generator inside a closed room?

options.text: The engine uses up all the nitrogen in the air
Carbon monoxide binds tightly to haemoglobin, so the blood can no longer carry oxygen
Petrol vapour dissolves the alveolar walls

questions.explanation: Incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide, which combines with haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin. That bond is roughly 250 times stronger than the oxygen bond and is effectively irreversible, so the affected haemoglobin is permanently taken out of service and the tissues are starved of oxygen.

distractorRationale.a: Nitrogen is not consumed by combustion and is not used by the body in that way
distractorRationale.c: Noise is a nuisance but not the cause of death in these cases
distractorRationale.d: Death results from oxygen starvation of the blood, not dissolution of the alveoli

questions.stem: Most of the carbon dioxide carried by blood is transported combined with haemoglobin inside the red blood cells.
questions.explanation: False. The bulk of carbon dioxide is carried dissolved in the plasma as hydrogencarbonate ions; only a small proportion combines with haemoglobin. Haemoglobin's main cargo is oxygen.

questions.stem: A person with a persistent bacterial infection is found to have a greatly raised white blood cell count. The most likely reason is that

options.text: white cells are needed to carry extra oxygen to the infected tissue
more phagocytes and lymphocytes are produced to engulf the bacteria and make antibodies
white cells help the blood to clot around the bacteria
the bacteria are multiplying inside the white cells

questions.explanation: White blood cells are the body's defence, so the bone marrow and lymph tissue step up production when bacteria are present. Phagocytes engulf and digest the invaders while lymphocytes multiply and secrete specific antibodies, and a raised count is used clinically as a sign of infection.

distractorRationale.a: Oxygen transport is the job of red cells, which contain haemoglobin
distractorRationale.c: Clotting is initiated by platelets, not white cells
distractorRationale.d: Bacteria taken into a phagocyte are digested, not cultured

questions.stem: State four functions of blood plasma and explain why a person of blood group O rhesus negative can donate red cells to a patient of any ABO group but can receive only group O rhesus negative blood.
markingGuide: Any four plasma functions, one mark each: transport of digested food such as glucose and amino acids; transport of excretory products such as urea and carbon dioxide; transport of hormones; distribution of heat around the body; transport of mineral salts; carriage of antibodies and clotting proteins
Donation explained: group O red cells carry neither antigen A nor antigen B, so no recipient antibody can agglutinate them (2 marks)
Reception explained: group O plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, so cells of group A, B or AB would be agglutinated (2 marks)

Rhesus factor explained: a rhesus negative recipient has no rhesus antigen and would form anti-rhesus antibodies if given rhesus positive blood, endangering later transfusions or pregnancies (2 marks)
questions.explanation: The two halves of the transfusion answer turn on different things: donation depends on the antigens on the donor's red cells, while reception depends on the antibodies in the recipient's plasma. The rhesus factor must be treated separately because it is a distinct antigen system from ABO.

questions.stem: What is the primary function of platelets in the blood?
questions.explanation: Platelets, or thrombocytes, are small cell fragments in the blood that play a crucial role in hemostasis, the process of blood clotting. They aggregate at the site of a blood vessel injury, helping to form a clot and prevent excessive bleeding.

distractorRationale.a: Red blood cells are responsible for transporting oxygen, not platelets.
distractorRationale.c: White blood cells are primarily responsible for fighting infections, while platelets are involved in clotting.
distractorRationale.d: Body temperature regulation is not a function of platelets.

questions.stem: Which component of blood is primarily responsible for the transport of carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation: Red blood cells (RBCs) are primarily responsible for the transport of carbon dioxide from the tissues back to the lungs. They carry carbon dioxide in two forms: dissolved in plasma and bound to hemoglobin.

distractorRationale.b: White blood cells are involved in immune responses, not in gas transport.
distractorRationale.c: While plasma carries some dissolved carbon dioxide, RBCs are the main transporters.
distractorRationale.d: Platelets are involved in clotting, not in gas transport.

questions.stem: In the ABO blood group system, which blood type can donate to all other blood types?
questions.explanation: Type O blood is known as the universal donor because it does not have A or B antigens on the surface of its red blood cells. This means it can be safely transfused to individuals of any ABO blood type without causing an immune reaction.

distractorRationale.b: Type A can only donate to Type A and AB recipients.
distractorRationale.c: Type B can only donate to Type B and AB recipients.
distractorRationale.d: Type AB can receive from all types but cannot donate to all types.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about plasma is true?

options.text: It is the liquid part of blood.
It contains only red blood cells.
It is responsible for immune response.

questions.explanation: Plasma is the liquid component of blood and makes up about 55% of its volume. It contains water, electrolytes, nutrients, hormones, and waste products, playing a vital role in transporting these substances throughout the body.

distractorRationale.b: Plasma contains red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets, not just red blood cells.
distractorRationale.c: While plasma contains antibodies, it is not solely responsible for immune response; white blood cells play a major role.
distractorRationale.d: Plasma is essential for transporting nutrients, including glucose and amino acids.

questions.stem: What is the role of hemoglobin in red blood cells?

options.text: To transport oxygen and carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Hemoglobin is a protein found in red blood cells that binds to oxygen in the lungs and carries it to tissues throughout the body. It also helps transport carbon dioxide from the tissues back to the lungs for exhalation.

distractorRationale.a: Fighting infections is primarily the role of white blood cells.
distractorRationale.c: Blood clotting is facilitated by platelets and fibrinogen, not hemoglobin.
distractorRationale.d: Blood pressure is regulated by the cardiovascular system, not directly by hemoglobin.

distractorRationale.a: Type O is the universal donor for red blood cells, not plasma.
distractorRationale.b: Type A plasma contains anti-B antibodies, which can react with type B blood.
distractorRationale.d: Type B plasma contains anti-A antibodies, which can react with type A blood.

questions.stem: What component of blood is primarily involved in the immune response?
questions.explanation: White blood cells (leukocytes) are the primary components of the immune system, responsible for defending the body against infections and foreign invaders. They identify and neutralize pathogens, playing a crucial role in maintaining health.

distractorRationale.a: Red blood cells are responsible for oxygen transport, not immune response.
distractorRationale.c: Plasma carries antibodies but is not directly involved in the immune response.
distractorRationale.d: Platelets are involved in blood clotting, not in fighting infections.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of Rh-positive blood?

options.text: It can receive blood from Rh-negative donors.
It can cause hemolytic disease in newborns.

questions.explanation: Rh-positive blood contains the Rh antigen on the surface of red blood cells, allowing individuals with this blood type to receive blood from Rh-negative donors without complications. However, they do not have anti-Rh antibodies unless sensitized.

distractorRationale.a: Rh-positive blood has Rh antigens present.
distractorRationale.c: Hemolytic disease of the newborn typically occurs when an Rh-negative mother has an Rh-positive baby.
distractorRationale.d: Rh-positive individuals do not produce anti-Rh antibodies unless they are sensitized.
